Speaking at a briefing on Ethiopia's participation in the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, Billene highlighted the country's progress in environmental protection, renewable energy expansion and preparations to host COP32 in 2027. She disclosed that Ethiopia has planted more than 56 billion seedlings over the past eight years under the Green Legacy Initiative. The Press Secretary described this the flagship national programme as a major contribution to global efforts to mitigate climate change and restore degraded ecosystems. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Billene stressed, however, that the initiative's success should not be measured by the number of seedlings planted alone, but also by their survival, continued care and protection to ensure lasting environmental benefits. She called for broader public participation in environmental conservation, emphasizing that nurturing and protecting planted trees must become a shared responsibility across all sections of society. She also recalled Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's repeated calls for citizens to take an active role in caring for planted trees to maximize their long-term environmental and economic benefits. Turning to Ethiopia's clean energy transition, Billene highlighted the country's expanding investments in hydropower, wind and solar energy to meet growing domestic electricity demand while strengthening its capacity to supply power to regional markets. She cited ongoing wind and solar projects as evidence of Ethiopia's efforts to diversify its renewable energy mix and advance a sustainable energy future. The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), she added, represents a major milestone in the country's renewable energy ambitions and electricity generation capacity. The landmark project will also be showcased at the Ethiopian Pavilion during COP31, she pointed out. Billene underscored that Ethiopia's investments in renewable energy, afforestation and environmental protection go beyond domestic development priorities, contributing to broader international efforts to address climate change and promote sustainable development. The briefing also highlighted Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's engagements at COP31, Ethiopia's preparations to host COP32 in 2027, and the country's plans to present its development achievements and climate action initiatives to the international community. The inhabitants further emphasized the need for consolidating progress toward lasting peace, stability and prosperity in the region. The call was made during a consultative forum of Mekelle residents, presided over by Chief of Staff of the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), Field Marshal Birhanu Jula. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Speaking at the gathering, Field Marshal Birhanu said the defunct TPLF faction had aligned itself with the so-called "Tsimdo" group, an alliance orchestrated by Ethiopia's historical adversaries to wage war against the country. He said his engagement with residents was aimed at fostering dialogue, strengthening cooperation and encouraging collective efforts to ensure lasting peace and stability in Tigray region. During the discussions, residents underscored their strong desire to see an end to conflict, identifying peace, security and sustainable development as their foremost priorities. They called for the reconstruction of damaged infrastructure, expanded employment opportunities for young people and the restoration of security to enable communities to resume normal life without fear. "Our foremost priorities are the reconstruction of critical infrastructure, the creation of meaningful employment opportunities for our youth, and the restoration of security so that citizens can go about their daily lives in peace," participants said. Residents also welcomed the resumption of salary payments for civil servants and ongoing infrastructure rehabilitation efforts, describing them as important steps toward restoring normalcy and accelerating the region's recovery. Concluding the forum, participants called on the Federal Government to maintain its commitment to Tigray, sustain ongoing interventions and accelerate reform, reconstruction and development initiatives to secure lasting peace and improve the livelihoods of communities across the region. The president’s remarks come against the backdrop of tensions surrounding Somaliland, which declared independence from Somalia in 1991 but has not secured widespread international recognition. Israel is the only country to have formally recognised Somaliland, while Taiwan maintains extensive diplomatic relations and a presence in the region’s capital, Hargeisa. Somalia considers Somaliland an integral part of its territory and has consistently opposed efforts to establish separate international recognition for the region. During his speech, Mr Mohamud also criticised opposition leaders, accusing them of seeking solutions through foreign intervention. He urged them to return to dialogue, calling for greater engagement on the country’s political challenges. The president returned to Mogadishu on Sunday after attending the COP31 United Nations climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye. During the conference, he warned that one of the strongest El Niño events recorded in Somalia could trigger severe flooding, potentially disrupting the lives of up to 3.4 million people in the country’s southern provinces. His comments highlighted the range of challenges facing Somalia, from diplomatic tensions over its territorial integrity to the growing threat of climate-related disasters. somalia.title: Power relations and agency in Somalia’s election process - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Power relations and agency in Somalia’s election process - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME OPINION Power relations and agency in Somalia’s election process Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Jamal Mohamed Sunday November 15, 2026 Somalia’s electoral history has been marked by significant shifts since independence. After gaining independence in 1960, the country held elections based on universal suffrage, including local elections in 1963 and parliamentary elections in 1964 and 1969 (Samatar 2015). This democratic period came to an end following the military coup led by Mohamed Siad Barre in 1969, which ushered in an authoritarian regime that lasted until the collapse of the state in 1991. Since then, Somalia has yet to hold a national election based on universal suffrage. The debate over elections in Somalia reflects a longstanding difference in approach. The international community (IC) has often advocated for universal suffrage, while Somali political actors have frequently relied on clan-based electoral arrangements. They argue that electoral systems need to take account of local political realities, historical experiences, and established ways of managing conflict. These differences are about more than voting procedures or institutional design. At their heart are deeper questions about who holds political authority, whose vision of legitimacy prevails, and how sovereignty, partnership, ownership, power, and agency are negotiated within Somalia’s state-building process. advertisements The choice of electoral system offers an important lens through which to examine how power and agency are negotiated between the IC and the Somali Government. Making sense of this debate requires looking beyond contemporary political disagreements and considering Somalia’s historical context. Lewis’s (1961) concept of pastoral democracy provides a useful starting point for exploring the roots of Somali political organisation and the continued influence of clan structures in governance. Lewis described pre-colonial Somali society as having indigenous systems of political organisation shaped by negotiation, consensus-building, collective decision-making, and authority dispersed among clan groups. In this context, political legitimacy was grounded less in formal state institutions and more in kinship ties, customary law, and agreements negotiated among clan elders and leaders (Lewis 1961). While the concept has been criticised for overlooking internal inequalities and placing too much emphasis on pastoral traditions, it remains influential in explaining the enduring role of clan politics and agency in Somali state-building. Clan-based electoral arrangements, therefore, should not be viewed simply as evidence of institutional weakness or democratic failure. They are rooted in a longer history of political organisation that predates colonial rule and the modern state (Lewis 1961). Following the collapse of the Somali state in 1991, and amid the absence of strong national institutions and a robust constitutional framework, clan structures also helped maintain social order, resolve disputes, and facilitate political negotiations (Gundel 2006). For many Somali political actors, these arrangements are consequently more than a temporary compromise. They remain a practical and, in some contexts, legitimate way of managing political competition in a fragmented political landscape. The IC, by contrast, has consistently supported a gradual shift towards elections based on universal suffrage. Since the establishment of successive transitional governments in the early 2000s, and particularly following the adoption of the Federal Constitution in 2012, universal suffrage has been presented as a means of strengthening political accountability and state legitimacy, widening citizen participation, and reducing the influence of clan identity in politics. This position is also shaped by ideas associated with liberal peacebuilding and neoliberal governance, which have informed international interventions in many post-conflict settings (Sharp 2018). These frameworks generally assume that sustainable peace and development can be advanced through liberal democratic institutions, competitive elections, market-oriented reforms, and formal mechanisms of accountability (Sharp 2018; De Coning 2007). From this perspective, universal suffrage is both a symbol and a tool of democratic transformation. However, these assumptions can overlook the complexity of local political contexts and risk prioritising externally promoted models of governance over forms of legitimacy grounded in local experience. Partnership and local ownership sit at the centre of the debate over Somalia’s electoral process. Both concepts have become prominent in development and aid discourse. Since the early 2000s, international organisations have increasingly stressed the importance of locally owned political processes in ensuring that external interventions are legitimate and sustainable. Local ownership, in principle, means that domestic actors lead decision-making while international partners provide support (Crawford 2003). Partnership similarly suggests a relationship built on mutual respect, shared goals, and joint responsibility. Yet these ideals do not always reflect the reality of donor–government relations, where significant imbalances in power often remain (Abrahamsen 2004). In practice, the language of partnership and local ownership can also serve as a way for different actors to advance their own interests in Somalia’s electoral process. The IC invokes these principles to legitimise its engagement and demonstrate its commitment to internationally accepted approaches to development. At the same time, it can shape the content, timing, and direction of electoral reforms through financial support, technical expertise, diplomatic pressure, and conditions attached to election-related assistance. This creates a paradox: partnership and local ownership are promoted within relationships where the IC may continue to exercise considerable influence. The Somali Government, however, is not simply a passive recipient of this influence. It also exercises agency by negotiating over election timelines, interpreting constitutional provisions, navigating political disagreements among actors, and invoking security concerns related to Al-Shabaab. These practices can affect both the pace and direction of the electoral process. Somali political actors also invoke local ownership and sovereignty to defend the continuation of clan-based electoral arrangements, which they may view as enjoying greater domestic legitimacy than externally advocated universal suffrage. These arguments, however, are not uncontested within Somalia. Some regard clan-based systems as necessary for maintaining political stability and preventing conflict, while others argue that they can reinforce established power structures and restrict meaningful participation by women, minority clans, young people, and other politically marginalised groups. This tension highlights that power and agency operate not only between the IC and the Somali Government, but also within Somali political institutions and society. They are neither fixed nor exercised in only one direction; rather, they are continually shaped through negotiation, resistance, and adaptation. Conclusion The Somali electoral process is shaped by competing understandings of political order. The IC often presents universal suffrage as essential to achieving long-term democratic development, while Somali political elites have frequently favoured negotiated, clan-based arrangements that reflect existing political realities and power structures. The disagreement is not merely about which electoral model should be adopted. It also concerns who should determine the country’s political future, what forms of representation are considered legitimate, and whether electoral reform should be guided primarily by international norms or by locally defined priorities. These competing visions continue to shape Somalia’s political transition. The Somali case therefore challenges simplistic partnership and localisation agendas between the IC and the government. It shows instead that state-building is a contested process in which international influence and domestic agency intersect, and in which power is continually negotiated. ______________________ Chief Officer Partnership & Coordination, County Government of Garissa. Since gaining independence in 1960, Somalia has experienced significant political shifts, transitioning from democratic elections to an authoritarian regime following the 1969 coup. The international community advocates for universal suffrage, while Somali political actors often favor clan-based electoral systems, reflecting local realities and historical experiences. This divergence raises questions about political authority and legitimacy within Somalia's state-building efforts. Clan structures, rooted in pre-colonial governance, continue to play a crucial role in maintaining social order and facilitating political negotiations. The international community's push for universal suffrage is seen as a means to enhance accountability and reduce clan influence, yet it risks overlooking local contexts. Ultimately, the Somali electoral process highlights the ongoing negotiation of power and agency, revealing tensions between international norms and locally defined priorities in shaping the country's political future.

The request reflects Mogadishu’s continued efforts to secure security and diplomatic support from Uganda. During Mohamud’s visit in late October, he asked Museveni to delay the withdrawal of Ugandan troops deployed under a bilateral agreement. Those forces have been holding key strategic towns in the Lower Shabelle region. The appeal was rejected and the drawdown has already started. It is not clear whether Mohamud would repeat the same request if the visit is approved, or whether he would raise other issues. Uganda has been one of the largest troop contributors to African Union missions in Somalia since 2007 and maintains a separate bilateral presence in sensitive areas. The latest outreach comes as Mohamud’s government faces a Supreme Court ruling that the extension of his term was unlawful. The court found that constitutional amendments lengthening presidential and parliamentary terms could not be applied to sitting officials whose original mandates had already expired. Separately, Mohamud has sent two special advisers to several countries to seek financial support from key African Union and European Union partners. The diplomatic efforts form part of a broader campaign to bolster his administration amid the political and security challenges facing Somalia. The agreement was signed in Antalya, Türkiye, on the sidelines of the COP31 United Nations climate conference by Somalia's Minister of Family and Human Rights Development, Khadija Mohamed Al-Makhzoumi, and Türkiye's Minister of Family and Social Services, Mahinur Özdemir Göktaş. advertisements According to Somalia's Ministry of Family and Human Rights Development, the agreement establishes a framework for cooperation in developing social welfare policies, exchanging expertise and strengthening services for vulnerable communities. The agreement covers the protection of women's and children's rights, prevention of violence against women and measures to safeguard children from risks associated with digital platforms and online environments. It also provides for cooperation in improving health and education services, along with care and rehabilitation programs for persons with disabilities and older people. The two governments agreed to organize training programs, conferences and seminars to strengthen the skills of social service professionals and facilitate the exchange of knowledge and experience. “The agreement is an important step toward improving Somalia's social services,” Al-Makhzoumi added, saying the government hopes to benefit from the experience of international partners, particularly Türkiye, in strengthening family protection and safeguarding the rights of women and children. The Somali minister also addressed a side event at COP31 focusing on the relationship between climate change, social protection and women's empowerment. She said recurring droughts and floods have severely affected Somali families, particularly women and children, who face increasing hardship as climate-related disasters disrupt livelihoods and access to essential services. Al-Makhzoumi called for international climate financing to reach the most vulnerable communities, especially rural families disproportionately affected by droughts and flooding. She also emphasized the importance of including women in the development of climate policies and adaptation strategies, highlighting their role in strengthening community resilience. The agreement comes as Somalia seeks greater international cooperation to improve social services and expand protection for communities affected by humanitarian emergencies and climate-related disasters. Türkiye has been one of Somalia's closest international partners since President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan visited Mogadishu in 2011 during a devastating drought and famine. Since then, Ankara has provided humanitarian assistance and supported projects in education, healthcare, infrastructure and institutional development. The two countries have also expanded cooperation in defense, military training, maritime security and energy development. The latest agreement broadens that relationship by placing greater emphasis on social welfare, family protection and support for vulnerable populations. (AP Photo/Abdel Kareem Hana) Mogadishu (HOL) — Somalia has joined 17 other Arab and Islamic countries in condemning an Israeli airstrike on the Nasser Medical Complex in southern Gaza, urging Israel to uphold the ceasefire, protect civilians and allow unrestricted humanitarian assistance into the Palestinian territory. In a joint statement issued Saturday, Nov. 14, the foreign ministers of the 18 countries said the strike on the hospital in Khan Younis caused casualties among patients and medical personnel and violated international humanitarian law, which provides special protection for healthcare facilities and workers. advertisements The statement was signed by the foreign ministers of Somalia, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman, Egypt, Jordan, Sudan, Libya, Palestine, Djibouti, Algeria, Lebanon, Mauritania, Türkiye, Pakistan and Indonesia. The ministers also condemned continued Israeli attacks on Palestinian civilians, including strikes on tents and other shelters housing displaced families. They warned that the attacks threaten the Gaza ceasefire and undermine international efforts to restore security and stability in the territory. The joint statement expressed serious concern over Israeli restrictions on humanitarian assistance, including essential medical supplies and shelter materials such as tents, caravans and mobile homes. The ministers said the restrictions were worsening Gaza's humanitarian crisis as winter approaches, leaving displaced families exposed to harsh weather conditions. They warned that inadequate shelter, deteriorating sanitation facilities and limited access to clean water and healthcare were placing civilians at serious risk, particularly children and infants. The foreign ministers called on Israel to immediately and fully implement its commitments under the Sharm el-Sheikh agreement, U.S. President Donald Trump's comprehensive peace plan and United Nations Security Council Resolution 2803 of 2025. They urged Israel to maintain the ceasefire, protect civilians and medical facilities, and ensure the safe, sustained and unrestricted delivery of humanitarian aid in sufficient quantities. The statement also called for the entry of equipment and supplies needed to restore essential infrastructure and support early recovery efforts in Gaza. The ministers emphasized that humanitarian assistance should not be delayed by political or security conditions or made dependent on progress in subsequent phases of the peace agreement. “We call on Israel to allow United Nations agencies and humanitarian organizations to carry out their operations without obstruction,” they added. The countries urged the United States and the Board of Peace to intensify diplomatic efforts to ensure Israel fulfills its commitments and removes restrictions on humanitarian aid entering Gaza. The ministers reaffirmed their determination to work with regional and international partners to strengthen the ceasefire, implement all phases of the peace plan and expand humanitarian assistance to Palestinians affected by the conflict. Somalia has repeatedly expressed support for Palestinian rights and joined Arab and Islamic countries in calling for an end to attacks on civilians and greater humanitarian access to Gaza. CEWARN, an IGAD mechanism established to support conflict prevention, works with member states to monitor indicators of instability, assess potential risks and facilitate timely responses. Somalia's hosting of the committee for the first time reflects its growing participation in regional initiatives aimed at promoting peace, stability and security. The meeting comes as countries in the Horn of Africa continue to face security challenges, including armed conflicts, political instability and competition over natural resources. IGAD provides a regional platform for cooperation on peace and security, economic integration and development among its member states.
